title: Delayed Intramyocardial Transplantation of Autologous Cardiac Atrial Stem Cells Attenuates Adverse Remodeling in Chronic Ischemic Cardiomyopathy
content: Background: Cell therapy for chronic ischaemic cardiomyopathy remains limited by poor myocardial retention and uncertain regenerative efficacy. We evaluated the effects of delayed intramyocardial transplantation of autologous cardiac atrial stem cells in a large-animal model of established chronic myocardial infarction. Methods: Myocardial infarction was induced in Göttingen minipigs by two-hour left anterior descending coronary artery occlusion. After two months of post-infarction remodeling, animals were randomly allocated to intramyocardial transplantation of autologous cardiac atrial stem cells or control treatment. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging and three-dimensional electromechanical mapping were performed before treatment and two months thereafter. Histological and immunofluorescence analyses assessed persistence and phenotype of transplanted cells. Results: At follow-up, left ventricular ejection fraction was preserved in treated animals but declined in controls (55 ± 9% versus 41 ± 7%; p = 0.0002). Treatment attenuated adverse ventricular remodeling, with preservation of end-systolic volume and regional wall thickening. Late gadolinium enhancement-defined infarct mass decreased from 6.2 ± 2.0 g to 4.0 ± 1.0 g in treated animals and was significantly lower than in controls at follow-up (p = 0.04). Electromechanical mapping demonstrated improved myocardial electrical viability and regional mechanical function. Transplanted cells persisted within the injured myocardium and exhibited cardiomyocyte-associated structural features. Conclusions: Delayed intramyocardial transplantation of autologous cardiac atrial stem cells attenuated adverse remodeling and was associated with improved regional myocardial structure and function in established chronic ischaemic cardiomyopathy.
